lesson.title: Stimulants: Turning Up the Nervous System's Volume
lesson.summary: Stimulants increase central nervous system activity through several different mechanisms, from boosting dopamine release to blocking the brain's own drowsiness signal.
lesson.body:
Stimulants are a class of psychoactive drugs that increase activity in the central nervous system, generally producing heightened alertness, a faster heart rate, and a subjective sense of energy or euphoria. Unlike a single neurotransmitter system, stimulants reach this outcome through several different mechanisms, which is why caffeine, nicotine, amphetamine, and cocaine all count as stimulants even though they act on different receptors and transporters.

Amphetamine and its relatives, including medications prescribed for ADHD, work mainly by increasing dopamine and norepinephrine activity. They prompt neurons to release extra dopamine and norepinephrine from their storage sites and also interfere with the transporters that would normally pull those chemicals back out of the synapse, echoing the reuptake blocking mechanism from the previous chapter. At carefully controlled therapeutic doses, this extra activity in brain regions tied to attention can improve focus for someone with ADHD, but at higher recreational doses the same mechanism produces euphoria and carries a real risk for misuse.

Cocaine, covered in the reuptake inhibitor chapter, reaches a similar dopamine surge purely by blocking reuptake rather than by forcing extra release, which helps explain why its effects come on quickly and fade quickly compared with amphetamine's longer, steadier action.

Caffeine works completely differently, and it is a useful example of an antagonist doing the stimulating rather than an agonist. Throughout the day, a molecule called adenosine gradually builds up in the brain and binds receptors that promote drowsiness by damping down neural firing. Caffeine has a shape similar enough to adenosine that it can occupy those same receptors without activating them, blocking adenosine from doing its job. The alertness people feel after coffee is really the brain's own accumulated sleepiness signal being muted, rather than an entirely new burst of energy being added.

Nicotine, finally, is a direct agonist at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, the same receptor type acetylcholine itself activates during ordinary attention and arousal, which is why it produces a quick sense of alertness and, with repeated use, is strongly tied to dependence. Nicotine is also a useful exception to the usual tolerance story covered later in this unit: chronic exposure typically causes nicotinic receptors to increase in number rather than decrease, even as the receptors themselves grow desensitized to constant stimulation, which is part of why cravings can resurface so quickly after just a few hours without a cigarette.

Taken together, stimulants show that a single behavioral outcome, feeling more awake and alert, can be produced by direct agonism, indirect agonism through blocked reuptake, or even by blocking an entirely separate inhibitory system. That variety is a useful reminder that a psychoactive drug's category describes what it does to behavior, not which specific mechanism it uses to get there.
